source_text: Si 'deus' commune uocabulum factum est uitio erroris humani, quatenus plures dei dicuntur atque creduntur in saeculo, benedictus tamen deus domini nostri Iesu Christi non alius quam creator intellegetur, qui et uniuersa benedixit — habes Genesim — et ab uniuersis benedicitur — habes Danihelem —; proinde si 'pater* potest dici sterilis deus, [nullius magis nomine quam creatoris] misericordiarum tamen pater idem erit, qui misericors et miserator et misericordiae plurimus dictus est. habes apud Ionam cum ipso misericordiae exemplum, quam Niniuitis exorantibus praestitit, facilis et Ezechiae fletibus flecti, et Achab, marito Iezabel, deprecanti sanguinem ignoscere Nabuthae, et Dauid agnoscenti delictum statim indulgens, malens scilicet paenitentiam peccatoris quam mortem, utique ex misericordiae adfectu. si quid tale Marcionis deus edidit uel edixit, agnoscam 'patrem misericordiarum'.
pass_a_gloss: If 'god' has become a common term due to the fault of human error, to the extent that many gods are said and believed in the world, nevertheless the blessed God of our Lord Jesus Christ is understood to be not other than the creator, who both blessed all things — you have Genesis — and is blessed by all things — you have Daniel —; therefore if 'father' can be said of a sterile god, [with no name more than that of the creator] nonetheless the father of mercies will be the same one who is said to be merciful and a mercifier and most full of mercies; you have with Jonah an example of his mercies, which he granted to the Ninevites when they prayed, easy to be bent by the tears of Hezekiah, and to Achab, the husband of Jezebel, forgiving the blood of Naboth when he prayed, and to David acknowledging his fault immediately giving indulgence, certainly preferring the repentance of the sinner to death, undoubtedly from an affection of mercy; if Marcion's god has produced or promulgated anything of this kind, I will acknowledge 'the father of mercies'

choices.english: God of our Lord Jesus Christ
choices.why: referring to the Christian concept of God
referring to God as a merciful father
referring to God as the creator of the world

pass_b_english: If "god" has become a generic label through the fault of human error, to the point that many gods are named and believed in throughout the world, the blessed God of our Lord Jesus Christ is still understood to be none other than the Creator—who both blessed all things (Genesis) and is blessed by all things (Daniel).

So even if "father" can be applied to a sterile god—with no title more distinctive than that of Creator—the Father of mercies will be the very same one who is called merciful, a mercifier, and most full of mercies.

You have an example of his mercies in Jonah: the mercy he granted the Ninevites when they prayed (Jonah); how easily he was moved by Hezekiah's tears; how he forgave Ahab, Jezebel's husband, the blood of Naboth when Ahab begged for it; how he immediately granted indulgence to David when David acknowledged his fault—plainly preferring the sinner's repentance to death, certainly out of an impulse of mercy.
If Marcion's god has ever produced or promulgated anything of that kind, I will acknowledge him as "the Father of mercies."

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a literal clause-by-clause translation, while Pass B provides a fluent rendering. Both correctly identify the scripture references (Genesis, Daniel, Jonah) and the specific biblical figures (Ninevites, Hezekiah, Ahab, Jezebel, Naboth, David). The distinction between the 'sterile god' and the 'father of mercies' is preserved. The bracketed text [nullius magis nomine quam creatoris] is handled correctly in both versions.
